description: Flat 8 m square of broom-finished poured concrete divided by a square grid of saw-cut expansion joints -- one quad, one seamless PBR texture set, tiling in both axes.

image.prompt:
A SEAMLESSLY TILING TOP-DOWN GROUND TEXTURE. This is a flat material swatch, not a photograph of a scene or of an object. The camera looks straight down at the ground from directly overhead, perfectly orthographic, with no perspective, no horizon, no vanishing point and no tilt.

The surface: Flat square of plain poured concrete hardstanding seen as a single unbroken surface, one continuous slab with NO joints, NO grooves and NO cut lines of any kind anywhere, finished all over with faint parallel broom-drag texture, gentle tonal drift and patchy grey staining, edge to edge concrete only, no kerb and no border Materials: Seamlessly tiling pale grey cast concrete with a fine broom-drag directional grain, bay-to-bay tonal drift from bone to mid grey where pours were made on different days, dark grit and moss packed into the saw-cut joints, hairline shrinkage cracks wandering across a few bays, oil and rust drip stains, chalky white efflorescence patches, damp dark blooms along the joints, scattered aggregate showing through worn patches and a few shallow spalled hollows; the joint grid must wrap on all four edges so a run of tiles gives continuous unbroken joint lines.

Scale: the square shown covers exactly 8 by 8 metres of real ground, so every stone, block, slab, joint, marking, rut and tuft in it is drawn at its true size relative to that. Do not zoom in on a detail and do not pull back to show a wider scene.

Tiling: the texture must repeat seamlessly on all four edges. What runs off the left edge continues onto the right edge, and what runs off the top continues onto the bottom, exactly. No feature may be cut in half at an edge without its other half appearing at the opposite edge. Laid out four by four this must read as one continuous surface with no visible grid, no repeated landmark feature and no seam.

Framing: the surface fills the entire frame edge to edge and corner to corner. There is no border, no frame, no margin, no backdrop, no background, no matte and no empty space of any kind. The ground continues past every edge of the image.

Nothing stands on it and nothing bounds it: no kerb, no wall, no step, no gutter, no drain, no manhole cover, no grass verge, no plants, no people, no vehicles, no furniture, no objects, no litter, no text, no labels, no watermarks, no measurement annotations, no arrows.

Lighting: flat, even, shadowless overhead illumination, like a lightbox. The image is the surface's true albedo. No sun, no cast shadows, no directional highlights, no specular blowout, no vignette, no gradient across the frame, no baked ambient occlusion in the corners and crevices, no light falloff towards the edges -- an uneven frame cannot tile, because its bright side would meet its dark side at every seam.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, realistic material, real surface wear and staining. Not stylised, not cartoon, not a 3D render preview, not a tiled collage of separate photographs, not a pattern illustration.

COMPOSITED AFTERWARDS by scripts/tilekit/composite.mjs, in metres on the 8 m frame: the geometry above is deliberately absent from the generated surface.

name: Poured Concrete Apron Tile
nameTh: พื้นคอนกรีต
notes: One flat quad, 8 x 8 m, lying in the ground plane at y=0 -- two triangles, one geometry, one draw call, one PBR material, and nothing else. The entire surface reads out of the texture; the saw-cut joints are a normal and AO groove rather than modelled geometry. This is the plainest member of the kit's ground-surface tile set and the one that covers the most ground in a Thai scene after the interlocking paver: car parks, petrol station forecourts, factory and warehouse yards, temple aprons, rice-drying slabs and the surface of any soi that was concreted rather than surfaced. Every tile in the ground set is 8 x 8 m, sits at y=0, uses pivot base-center and snaps on the kit's 8 m grid, so it butts flush against any other ground tile and against the asphalt road tiles, and the raised Concrete Sidewalk Strip (2.0 m wide, 0.15 m tall) sits alongside as a separate object. The expansion joints form a SQUARE grid whose pitch must divide 8 m evenly and wrap on all four edges, which makes the tile fully FOUR-way rotationally symmetric -- it drops in at any of four orientations, and that plus the bay-to-bay tonal drift is what stops a large yard reading as a grid of identical copies. A broken joint line at a tile boundary is the first thing to check on the generated texture. Two things this tile is deliberately NOT: it carries no drain channels, no lid slabs and no edge bands, which is what separates it from the kit's older soi-alley-straight-tile, a 4 x 8 m alley piece with an open side drain painted into it; and it carries no road markings. One risk specific to this tile: flat pale grey concrete can land very close to the reference plate's grey backdrop and confuse a silhouette gate, so the generated plate needs real bay-to-bay tonal variation and staining rather than one even grey. Budget overridden explicitly to 2 triangles / 1 draw call / 1 material / 1 unique geometry instead of the hero2x its 8 m footprint would derive: footprint drives the class, but there is no geometry here to spend a class budget on. No destruction groups: a ground tile is static level geometry, not a breakable. The rigid geometry on this tile is NOT generated: six seeds of the apron grid and one of the lane markings landed the pattern off the 8 m frame, breaking it at every boundary, so prompts.image asks the generator for the bare SURFACE only and scripts/tilekit/composite.mjs draws the geometry afterwards at known coordinates in metres. That is what makes the pitch divide 8 m and the lines wrap exactly, by construction rather than by luck, and it is the same split scripts/tilekit/substrates.mjs already uses for the road markings.
